html:
"Sardinia-Piedmont" is the map's label, from 1650 to 1715, for the lands of the dukes of Savoy: Savoy in the western Alps, Piedmont around Turin and the county of Nice. They did not hold Sardinia until 1720, so the label looks ahead.

The House of Savoy controlled key passes over the Alps between France and Italy. The emperor made its count a duke in 1416. France occupied most of the duchy in the 1530s; Duke Emmanuel Philibert won it back in 1559 and moved the capital from Chambéry over the mountains to Turin in 1563, turning the state toward Italy. Earlier maps show this state as Savoy.

Squeezed between France and Spain, the dukes changed sides as it suited them. Victor Amadeus II joined the alliance against Louis XIV, survived the French siege of Turin in 1706, and at the Peace of Utrecht in 1713 won Sicily and a royal crown. In 1720 he had to swap Sicily for Sardinia, and the state became the Kingdom of Sardinia, which later united Italy.
